note: arXiv 1908.02983 (Arazo et al., 'Pseudo-Labeling and Confirmation Bias in Deep Semi-Supervised Learning'). The abstract contains both quotes and uses soft pseudo-labels; mixup and a minimum number of labeled samples per mini-batch are named as the regularizers. The arXiv page lists no venue, so I treated it as a preprint; I believe it appeared at IJCNN 2020, but I did not confirm that. The results are on generic SSL image benchmarks (CIFAR, Mini-ImageNet etc.), not agriculture.

arXiv 2112.06586 (MaskAL), peer-reviewed in Computers and Electronics in Agriculture vol. 197 (2022). The abstract confirms a broccoli dataset with 5 visually similar classes, Mask R-CNN, 900 vs 2300 images, 93.9% of full performance with 17.9% of the data vs random's 81.9% with 16.4%, and a 14,000-image full training set. The 'disease/defect' label is a gloss: the abstract only says 5 classes. The result is for a single dataset.

arXiv 2006.04255, preprint with no venue listed (checked the ar5iv full text). Two errors. (1) The initial labeled set is a random batch of 1000 samples spread across classes, not a 5% seed; the 5% is a randomly selected validation split. (2) Not all four methods beat random on both datasets: on soybean (8 stress classes + healthy, indoor imaging with constant illumination), Least Confidence, Entropy and DBAL beat random but Coreset did worse than random. On the field weed dataset (9 species), all four beat random. The abstract's general statement that AL beats random overstates the Coreset result.

arXiv 1911.10317 (PlantDoc), peer-reviewed at CoDS-COMAD 2020 (ACM). The abstract confirms 'up to 31%', 2,598 images (9,216 cropped leaf boxes), 13 species, 27 classes (17 disease). The paper words the gain both as accuracy and, in the intro, as error reduction. From the tables, the closest match is InceptionResNetV2 trained on PlantVillage only, 39.87% on field images, vs 70.53% after fine-tuning on PlantDoc, about +30.7 pp. VGG16 shows a larger gap (19.73% to 60.41%), so the paper's 'up to 31%' is loose. 'Small amount of field data matters' is an interpretation, but the lab-to-field framing fits.
